opus-5.5.text:
I think what's really striking about how OpenAI handled Sora is how much they trusted a very small group of people. When you look at it from the outside, people assume something like Sora must come from a huge organization with hundreds of researchers. But my impression is that the core of it was a small, very focused team. They were given a lot of freedom, and also a lot of compute, and that combination is quite rare.

Bill Peebles, who I worked with on the Diffusion Transformer, DiT, was one of the people leading it. When we did DiT, it was a fairly academic project. We were asking a simple question: can we replace the U-Net backbone in diffusion models with a transformer, and does it scale the way transformers scale in language? The answer turned out to be yes, quite cleanly. But in an academic setting, you can only push that so far. You show the scaling trend, you write the paper, and that's it.

What OpenAI did was say: okay, if this scaling trend is real, let's actually bet on it. Let's go all the way. That kind of conviction is something I really respect. A lot of organizations have the resources, but they spread them across many directions, or they need a lot of justification before committing. OpenAI has this culture of picking a direction they believe in and then concentrating resources behind it, even when it's not obvious it will work.

Another thing is the patience. Sora wasn't a product sprint. It took time, and they let the researchers keep working on fundamental questions like data, how you represent video as patches, how you handle different resolutions and durations, rather than forcing them to ship something early.

Of course, there's another side. That model of research is also quite closed. A lot of the details aren't shared, and as someone who cares about the open research community, I sometimes feel a bit conflicted about that. Progress in this field has historically come from people building on each other's work openly. DiT itself was open, and I think that's partly why it got adopted so widely.

So overall, I think their approach shows what is possible when you combine a simple, scalable idea, a small and talented team, and a strong institutional willingness to bet big. But I also think the academic community and the open community still have a very important role, especially in asking the questions that aren't just about scaling, like what these models actually understand about the world, and whether video generation is really the path to world models or just one piece of it.

r001.rationale: It describes Sora as coming from a small, focused research team given substantial freedom and compute, which conveys a bottom-up effort.

r002.rationale: It says OpenAI committed resources to pursue the DiT scaling idea, but does not say the team pursued ambitions previously considered unthinkable.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention FAIR or compare its organizational culture with OpenAI’s.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that Sora was not primarily a research project in the way academics usually mean it. It was an engineering effort, a product effort, and the research was in service of that. And OpenAI's approach reflects that very clearly.

What they did well, honestly, is that they made a bet. They took a direction, the diffusion transformer, scaling it up on video, and they committed real resources to it. That's something a university lab simply can't do. When I was working on DiT with Bill Peebles, we had a handful of GPUs. We could show that the architecture scales nicely, that the inductive biases from the U-Net weren't necessary, but we couldn't actually push it to the point where you see these emergent behaviors in video. OpenAI could. They put the compute, the data pipeline, the infrastructure, the people behind it, and that's how you go from a paper to something like Sora.

The other thing I'd point to is that they let a small team move fast. From what I understand, Sora was built by a fairly small group, and they weren't bogged down by having to publish every intermediate result or justify every decision to a review committee. That's a huge advantage. In academia, a lot of our energy goes into writing papers and getting them accepted, and that process rewards incremental, defensible contributions rather than big swings.

Where I have mixed feelings is the openness side. The technical report for Sora was quite thin. It gestured at spacetime patches, at scaling, at the world simulator framing, but there wasn't enough detail for the community to reproduce or build on it. So it was a demonstration more than a contribution to the shared body of knowledge. And I understand the reasons, competitive and safety concerns, but as a researcher it's frustrating. A lot of the ideas in there came out of open research, including our work, and the loop back to the open community was pretty weak.

So my view is twofold. As a model of how to turn a research idea into a frontier system, their approach is very effective, focused, well-resourced, decisive. As a model of how to support the research ecosystem, it's much less so. And I think that gap matters, because the next DiT, the next idea that becomes a Sora, is probably going to come from somewhere outside OpenAI, and it depends on that ecosystem staying healthy.

r001.rationale: The response describes OpenAI making a strategic bet and giving a small team room to move quickly, but it does not characterize the effort as bottom-up.

r002.rationale: It says a university lab could not scale DiT to reveal emergent video behaviors, while OpenAI supplied the compute, data pipeline, infrastructure, and people to do so.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention FAIR or compare its organizational culture with OpenAI’s support for Sora.

astra-6.text:
What stands out to me is the willingness to commit substantial resources to a research direction whose outcome is uncertain. For something like Sora, you need more than a promising idea—you need compute, infrastructure, and time to experiment. Supporting that work means giving researchers room to find out what actually works.

I don’t have visibility into OpenAI’s internal decisions, so I wouldn’t want to speculate about how the project was managed. But I think the broader lesson is that ambitious research depends on an organization’s ability to sustain that uncertainty. You can’t demand a predictable product milestone from every experiment.

r002.rationale: It credits organizational support with resources and time, but does not say this enabled the Sora team to pursue ambitions previously considered unthinkable.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention FAIR or compare its organizational culture with OpenAI’s support for Sora.

sol-6.1.text:
What stands out to me is the willingness to invest in a research direction whose payoff is uncertain. With something like Sora, you need more than a promising idea. You need computing resources, data infrastructure, and people who can work together over a long period. Supporting that effort means giving researchers room to explore before there is a clear product.

I don’t have visibility into OpenAI’s internal decisions, so I wouldn’t claim to know exactly how they organized it. But I think the broader lesson is that ambitious research depends on an institution being willing to sustain that uncertainty.
